extracted.intended_audience: advanced high-school or undergraduate students of mathematics; readers of a mathematics textbook (e.g., 'What Is Mathematics?')
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter material giving definitions, theorems, and constructive procedures for algebraic vs transcendental numbers, the algebra of sets (Boolean laws and their use in logic), basic probability via set operations, and the characterization of ruler-and-compass constructible numbers and polygons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Algebraic number
rubrics_metrics.description: An algebraic number is any number x, real or complex, that satisfies some algebraic equation of the form a_n x^n + a_{n-1} x^{n-1} + ... + a_1 x + a_0 = 0 (n > 1, a_n ≠ 0) where the a_i are integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: √2 is algebraic since it satisfies x^2 - 2 = 0. Rational numbers are the special case n = 1. Any root of an integer-coefficient polynomial (any degree) is algebraic, regardless of expressibility by radicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Transcendental number
rubrics_metrics.description: A transcendental number is a real number that is not algebraic; i.e., it does not satisfy any nontrivial polynomial equation with integer coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cantor's denumerability argument shows transcendental numbers exist because algebraic numbers are countable while reals are uncountable. Important problems: proving specific numbers such as π and e are transcendental (discussed later in the book).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's enumeration method for algebraic numbers (existence of transcendentals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign to each polynomial a positive integer 'height' h = |a_n| + |a_{n-1}| + ... + |a_1| + |a_0| + n; for fixed h only finitely many integer-coefficient polynomials exist, each with at most n roots, so algebraic numbers are countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange algebraic numbers by increasing height to form a sequence; since reals are uncountable, some reals are not algebraic (transcendental). The construction is non-constructive in the sense of explicit decimal expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liouville's theorem (approximation bound for algebraic numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: If z is an algebraic number of degree n > 1, then z cannot be approximated 'too well' by rationals: for any sequence of rationals p/q approaching z, the inequality |z - p/q| < 1/q^{n+1} cannot hold for all sufficiently large q; equivalently, |z - p/q| > 1/q^{n+1} for sufficiently large denominators q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is proved by applying the polynomial f(x) with integer coefficients that vanishes at z to a nearby rational p/q, bounding f(p/q) both by a nonzero integer numerator and by a small real bound M/q^{n+1}, leading to |z - p/q| >= 1/q^{n+1} for large q. This rules out extremely close rational approximations to algebraic numbers and is used to construct transcendental numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of explicit transcendental (Liouville) numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Liouville constructed numbers whose decimal expansions are specially chosen (for example sums of terms like 10^{-m!}) so that they can be approximated by rationals far more closely than allowed by Liouville's inequality for algebraic numbers; such numbers are therefore transcendental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example construction: z = Σ_{m=1}^∞ 10^{-m!} (or similar factorial-based denominators). For sufficiently large m the approximation by truncating the series yields |z - p/q| < 1/q^{n+1} for arbitrarily large q, contradicting Liouville's theorem if z were algebraic; hence z is transcendental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements on approximation exponents (Thue and Siegel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stronger results than Liouville's original exponent n+1 have been proved: Thue showed the exponent may be replaced by (n/2)+1, and Siegel proved even sharper statements (the text states an exponent 2√n) for large n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These results refine how well algebraic numbers of degree n can or cannot be approximated by rationals and lead into Diophantine approximation and transcendence theory (Gelfond, Siegel, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Set and subset
rubrics_metrics.description: A set is defined by a property S1: the objects that possess that property form the set A. A is a subset of B (write A ⊆ B) if there is no object in A that is not also in B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: If I is the integers, A might be even integers, B odd integers. Include as subsets the universe I itself and the empty set ∅. Equality A = B means each is a subset of the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 1: Reflexivity of subset relation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every set is a subset of itself; obvious from the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 2: Antisymmetry / equality from mutual inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: 2) If A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A, then A = B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mutual inclusion implies set equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 3: Transitivity of subset relation
rubrics_metrics.description: 3) If A ⊆ B and B ⊆ C, then A ⊆ C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subset relation is transitive, analogous to ≤.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 4: Empty set is subset of every set
rubrics_metrics.description: 4) ∅ ⊆ A for any set A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the empty set contains no elements, it vacuously satisfies subset property for any A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 5: Every set is subset of the universe
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By definition of universe of discourse I; every subset is contained in I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Union and intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: Union (A + B) is the set of objects in either A or B (including both). Intersection (AB or A·B) is the set of objects in both A and B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 6: Commutativity of union
rubrics_metrics.description: 6) A + B = B + A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order doesn't matter for union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 7: Commutativity of intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: 7) AB = BA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order doesn't matter for intersection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 8: Associativity of union
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grouping doesn't change union of multiple sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 9: Associativity of intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: 9) A(BC) = (AB)C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grouping doesn't change intersection of multiple sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 10: Idempotence of union
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union of a set with itself is itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 11: Idempotence of intersection
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intersection of a set with itself is itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 12: Distributive law (intersection over union)
rubrics_metrics.description: 12) A(B + C) = AB + AC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intersection distributes over union; analogous to multiplication distributing over addition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 13: Distributive law (union over intersection)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union distributes over intersection (dual distributive law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 14: Union with empty set
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union with the empty set leaves A unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 15: Intersection with universe
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intersection with the universe I leaves A unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 16: Union with universe
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Union with the universe yields the universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 17: Intersection with empty set
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intersection with the empty set is empty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 18: Subset equivalences using union/intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: 18) The relation A ⊆ B is equivalent to either of the two relations A + B = B or AB = A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These algebraic equalities provide alternative characterizations of subset relation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 19: Law of excluded middle (set form)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every element of the universe is either in A or in its complement A'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 20: Law of contradiction (set form)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No object can be both in A and its complement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 21: Complement of empty set
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement of empty set is the entire universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 22: Complement of universe
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement of universe is empty set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 23: Double complement
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking complement twice returns the original set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 24: Order reversal under complement
rubrics_metrics.description: 24) The relation A ⊆ B is equivalent to the relation B' ⊆ A'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement reverses subset ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 25: De Morgan's law for union
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement of a union is intersection of complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law 26: De Morgan's law for intersection
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement of an intersection is union of complements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duality principle in algebra of sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Any law obtained from laws 1–26 by interchanging 0 and I, + and ·, and (where they appear) priming operations, yields another valid 'dual' law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: law 6 (A + B = B + A) dualizes to law 7 (AB = BA). Proofs map step-by-step via corresponding dual laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebra of sets as algebra of logic (translation rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translation between set notation and logical statements: 'All A are B' or 'If A then B' corresponds to A ⊆ B; 'Some A are B' corresponds to AB ≠ ∅; 'No A are B' corresponds to AB = ∅; 'Some A are not B' corresponds to AB' ≠ ∅; 'Not A' corresponds to A'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these correspondences to convert syllogisms into algebraic set equalities (e.g., Barbara: if A ⊆ B and B ⊆ C then A ⊆ C). The laws 19 and 20 correspond to excluded middle and contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boolean algebra axiomatization (three axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of the algebra of sets (1–26) can be deduced from a smaller set of axioms (three statements cited as 27) taken as axioms), enabling construction of Boolean algebra as a deductive system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With + and ' as primitive operations, intersection and order can be defined; this gives an axiomatic basis for Boolean algebras (see text for the three base axioms and the definitions AB ≡ (A' + B')' and A ⊆ B ≡ A + B = B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Probability via finite equally-likely outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: For an experiment with finite equally-likely outcomes and universe I, the probability of event A is P(A) = n(A)/n(I), where n(·) denotes number of elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In a 52-card deck, P(hearts) = 13/52 = 1/4. This set-based definition underpins classical probability calculations in finite sample spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion-exclusion for two sets
rubrics_metrics.description: P(A + B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(AB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: elements in AB are counted twice in P(A) + P(B) and must be subtracted once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion-exclusion for three sets
rubrics_metrics.description: P(A + B + C) = P(A) + P(B) + P(C) - P(AB) - P(AC) - P(BC) + P(ABC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by iterating the two-set formula and using distributivity ( (A + B)C = AC + BC ). Example: probability at least one digit in correct place when permuting 1,2,3.

rubrics_metrics.name: General inclusion-exclusion formula (n sets)
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of the union of n sets equals the alternating sum over all k-fold intersections: P(⋃_{i=1}^n A_i) = Σ P(A_i) - Σ P(A_i A_j) + Σ P(A_i A_j A_k) - ... with summation over all combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may be established by mathematical induction; applied to permutations to compute probability that at least one digit is fixed (derangement-related sums).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability example: fixed-point probability for permutations
rubrics_metrics.description: If the digits 1..n are written in random order, the probability that at least one digit occupies its proper place equals 1 - 1/1! + 1/2! - 1/3! + ... ± 1/n! → 1 - 1/e as n → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For n=3 the probability is 2/3; for n=5 it's approximately 0.63333; limit as n→∞ is 1 - 1/e ≈ 0.63212.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructible quantity principle (ruler-and-compass)
rubrics_metrics.description: From given segments a, b, c, ... one can construct by ruler and compass any quantity obtainable from them by rational operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and by successive extraction of square roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric constructions correspond to algebraic operations: constructing a ± b, ra (r rational), a/b, and ab are elementary (via marking and similar triangles); extraction of √a is done by circle/diameter/right-triangle construction (figure referenced). The total set obtainable is a number field closed under rational operations and square roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction procedure paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Every geometric construction problem can be translated to algebra: express the required segment x in an equation relating x to given quantities a, b, c, ...; solve algebraically and then decide whether the solution can be obtained by the allowed geometric operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analytic-geometry perspective reduces constructibility questions to algebraic characterization of solutions and whether they can be obtained by repeated rational operations and square-root extractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric construction operations examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary geometric constructions: (i) construct a + b and a - b by concatenation on a line; (ii) construct rational multiples a/q via similar triangles; (iii) construct ab and a/b via parallel-line/similarity constructions; (iv) construct √a using a circle with diameter of length a+1 and right-triangle similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures 27–31 in text illustrate these classical constructions; they justify that rational algebraic operations are implementable by ruler and compass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Number field generated by given segments
rubrics_metrics.description: The totality of quantities obtainable from given numbers a, b, c, ... by repeated application of rational operations forms a number field generated by those numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding the ability to take square roots extends the field further; this algebraic viewpoint underlies proofs of impossibility for certain constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gauss criterion for constructible regular p-gons
rubrics_metrics.description: Gauss's result: the regular p-gon (p a prime) is constructible with ruler and compass if and only if p is a Fermat prime of form p = 2^{2^s} + 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Fermat primes: 3, 5, 17, 257, 65537. This provides a concrete algebraic criterion deciding which regular polygons are constructible in principle (not minimal-step constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical/technical caveat on ruler use
rubrics_metrics.description: The ruler is used only as a straightedge for drawing lines, not for measuring or marking distances; the restriction to ruler and compass is a theoretical limitation dating to antiquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing other instruments (e.g., a right-angle or markings) changes the class of constructible problems; the textbook concentrates on classical ruler-and-compass constructibility as a theoretical notion.
